title: Pricing Decisions & Target Costing — How MBG Bids a Job (CMA P2-C · feeds BAR)
lessonHtml:
Cold open — markup on cost is not the same as margin on price

MBG bids work two ways: build the price up from cost (cost-plus) or start from what the market will pay and design the cost down to fit (target costing). The single most common pricing error — on the exam and on real bids — is confusing a markup on cost with a margin on price. This week makes the distinction precise and computes both, plus the target-costing discipline.

Cost-plus (markup on cost)

Markup on cost applies a percentage to the job cost. With an illustrative job cost of $300,000 and a 20% markup: bid = $300,000 × (1 + 0.20) = $360,000. The $60,000 markup is 20% of cost but only $60,000 ÷ $360,000 = 16.7% of the price. Cost-plus is simple and common in change orders and time-and-materials work, but it does not guarantee the market will accept the price.

Margin on price

A target margin on price is solved differently: price = cost ÷ (1 − margin). To earn a 20% margin on price from the same $300,000 cost: price = $300,000 ÷ (1 − 0.20) = $300,000 ÷ 0.80 = $375,000. Notice it is higher than the $360,000 from a 20% markup on cost — because 20% of the (larger) price is more dollars than 20% of cost. To earn a 25% margin on price: $300,000 ÷ 0.75 = $400,000, the spec-home price from week 1. Always confirm whether a percentage is stated on cost or on price.

Target costing — design to cost

Target costing reverses the logic: start with the price the market sets, subtract the required profit, and the remainder is the cost the product must hit.

Target cost = target price − required profit.

Illustrative: the market price is $400,000 and MBG requires a 15% margin = $60,000. Target cost = $400,000 − $60,000 = $340,000. If the current expected cost is $360,000, MBG must engineer $20,000 out of the design — value engineering, supplier negotiation, scope or method changes — before committing. Target costing pushes cost discipline to the design stage, where most cost is locked in, rather than discovering an overrun after the slab is poured.

Other pricing considerations

Bid pricing also weighs competition, capacity (a busy contractor bids higher), strategic value of the client, and risk. Change-order pricing follows the contract's agreed markup on added cost and is a major profit lever — disciplined change-order documentation and pricing recover costs that would otherwise erode margin. Predatory or below-cost pricing carries legal and reputational risk and is generally avoided.

Three pricing approaches and the product life cycle

Pricing methods sit on a spectrum. Cost-based pricing (cost-plus, the markup math above) is simple and defensible for cost-reimbursable and change-order work but ignores what the market will bear. Market-based pricing starts from competitors and the customer's alternatives — essential in competitive bidding, where the low responsible bid often wins. Value-based pricing sets price from the value delivered to the customer (speed, quality, a guaranteed completion date), and captures the most margin when the contractor can differentiate. Most real bids blend all three: a cost floor, a market ceiling, and a value-based position in between.

New offerings also follow a life-cycle choice between skimming (a high introductory price to capture early high-value buyers, then lower it) and penetration (a low price to win share quickly and deter entrants). Skimming suits a differentiated or capacity-constrained builder; penetration suits a commoditized market where volume and scale matter.

Elasticity and the legal guardrails

Price elasticity of demand governs how far price can move: where demand is elastic (many substitutes, price-sensitive owners), a price increase loses more volume than it gains in margin, so the profit-maximizing move is often to hold or cut; where demand is inelastic (a specialized, time-critical, or sole-qualified job), there is room to price for value. An analyst pairs elasticity with the contribution margin to find the price that maximizes total contribution, not just the highest price the market will tolerate.

Pricing is also legally bounded: predatory pricing (below cost to drive out competitors), price fixing with competitors, and certain forms of price discrimination between buyers can violate competition law. And target costing closes the loop on all of it — if the market price is fixed at $400,000 and the firm requires a $60,000 margin, the $340,000 target cost is non-negotiable, so the lever shifts from price to cost engineering: value engineering the design, renegotiating supplier terms, or changing methods until the cost fits the price the market has already set.

Contract structures and a worked pricing trade-off

How a contractor is paid shapes the pricing decision. A fixed-price (lump-sum) contract puts cost-overrun risk on MBG, so the bid must build in contingency and the markup math must be conservative. A cost-plus contract (cost plus a fee — fixed fee, or a percentage) shifts cost risk to the owner and rewards documented cost, which is why owners cap it and audit it. A guaranteed-maximum-price contract blends the two, with shared savings below the cap. The pricing method follows the structure: cost-plus and change orders use cost-based markups, while competitive lump-sum work is market-driven with a value-based edge where MBG can differentiate.

A worked trade-off shows why elasticity matters. Suppose at $400,000 MBG expects to sell 24 homes (contribution $100,000 each, total $2,400,000), and a 10% price cut to $360,000 raises volume to 30 homes but drops contribution to $60,000 each — total contribution $1,800,000. Despite selling more, the price cut destroys $600,000 of contribution because demand was not elastic enough to offset the thinner margin. Run the same numbers with a jump to 45 homes and the cut would pay off. The point is that price changes must be evaluated on total contribution, never on volume or revenue alone.

Finally, a contractor's pricing discipline includes the bid/no-bid decision itself. Preparing a competitive bid is costly, and chasing work that is mispriced, outside core competence, or likely to go to a lower-cost competitor wastes estimating capacity that could win better jobs. The same relevant-cost thinking applies: bid when the expected contribution, weighted by the probability of winning, exceeds the cost of bidding and the opportunity cost of the capacity the job would consume. Pricing, in other words, starts before the number is set — with the choice of which work to price at all.

CPA Crossover — BAR

BAR tests both pricing directions and especially the markup-versus-margin distinction, plus target-cost computation. Expect a question that gives a margin "on sales" and tempts you to apply it as a markup on cost — the wrong answer by design.

Practice and recap

  1. Compute a cost-plus bid as cost × (1 + markup).
  2. Compute a price for a target margin as cost ÷ (1 − margin).
  3. Distinguish markup on cost from margin on price every time.
  4. Compute target cost as price − required profit and size the gap to close.

Recap: a 20% markup on a $300,000 cost bids $360,000, while a 20% margin on price requires $375,000 and a 25% margin requires $400,000. Target costing works backward from a $400,000 market price to a $340,000 target cost, demanding $20,000 of design savings.

flashcards.back: Price = cost ÷ (1 − margin); $300,000 ÷ 0.80 = $375,000 for a 20% margin.

flashcards.front: Why is a 20% margin priced higher than a 20% markup?
flashcards.back: 20% of the larger price is more dollars than 20% of cost ($375,000 vs $360,000).

flashcards.front: Price for a 25% margin on a $300,000 cost

flashcards.back: Target cost = target (market) price − required profit.

flashcards.front: How much design savings if current cost is $360,000?

flashcards.back: It enforces cost discipline at the design stage, where most cost is locked in.

Why does a 20% margin on price exceed a 20% markup on cost?
choices: 20% of the larger price is more dollars than 20% of cost
questions.explain: Margin is taken on the price base, which is larger, so the dollar profit (and price) is higher.

If the current expected cost is $360,000 and the target cost is $340,000, MBG must:
choices: Engineer $20,000 of cost out of the design
questions.explain: Target costing requires closing the $20,000 gap through design/value engineering before committing.

questions.q: To earn a 25% margin on price from a $300,000 cost, the price is:
Target costing differs from cost-plus because it:
choices: Starts from the market price and designs cost down to fit
questions.explain: Target costing is market-driven: price − required profit = the cost the design must achieve.
